One question for "what needs doing", across the three stores that hold it
chief-of-staff 05
5dd99ad · 8 files
chief-of-staff 05. Kevin asked his chief of staff to advise on "my stuff that needs doing, errands" and that turned out to live in three places with nothing asking all three at once: checklists with their per-day ticks, list_items reminders, and events where kind = TASK. HomeDigestBuilder already answers a different question - how is each aspect doing - by reading the aspect digests. This answers what is outstanding right now, which is what a chief-of-staff reply to "what should I be doing" has to be built from rather than each advisor re-deriving it. The ranking is the design, and it is by when a thing stops being possible, never by which table it came from. Overdue first, with the MOST overdue leading - something ignored longest is more likely forgotten than deferred. Then dated, soonest first. Then undated errands. Then today's already-ticked lines, listed last rather than dropped, because a finished day should read as finished rather than as empty: section 1's empty-versus-unreadable distinction pointed at a day's work. A checklist line is never overdue. It resets tonight, so it cannot be late, only unticked - and conflating the two would put a bio line it is still 9am to do in the same bucket as a coursework deadline that passed, which is the exact flattening this module exists to avoid. A checklist that cannot be READ is skipped rather than rendered as an empty one, for the same reason. The judgement is pure and the fetching is not: Outstanding.kt has no Android in it and carries every ordering decision, OutstandingController only gathers. That split is what lets ten tests pin the ranking without Room or a device, including the failure this exists to prevent - three lists stapled end to end, so an undated errand outranks a deadline that passed purely because of which table it came from. 3518 tests, 0 failures. Owed: nothing calls it yet. It is the input the advisor and a screen should both read, and wiring either is the next step rather than part of this one. Kevin, 2026-09-12: "the direction i actually wanna go is alfred will be the executive of my estate, my chief of staff. advise me on my net worth, my stuff that needs doing, errands, schoolwork, advise on career everything." Checked before charting, and the honest answer is that this is largely built. aspect-advisors is 21 tickets and every one is resolved: five advisors, and HomeDigestBuilder is explicitly the cross-aspect one - one headline per aspect, the gap that matters, any goal visibly off track. That IS the chief-of-staff shape. AdvisorProposalExecutor is an allowlisted write door, so the advisor can already ACT with Kevin accepting first. The playbooks carry real doctrine. CredPlaybook already draws the finance line and draws it correctly: not a licensed advisor, never recommends securities, funds, tickers or allocations, account types named only generically. Nothing here reopens it, and "advise me on my net worth" does not need it reopened - telling Kevin what he is worth is reporting, telling him what to buy is advice. Four gaps. Net worth does not exist at all - no assets, no liabilities, anywhere. Ledger holds transactions and bank balances; fleet holds cars with no value. And this is the one to be careful with, because a net worth would be the FIRST figure LEGION shows that mixes provenance: a reconciled checking balance, a guessed car value, a hand-typed 401k, a loan balance that decays silently. Summing those and rendering one number is exactly what section 4 rules 5 and 7 forbid, and it is also the most quotable figure the app will ever produce - a number a person repeats to someone else. The map proposes a net worth is never one number: the figure plus, in words, how much of it rests on estimates. Career is not an aspect and section 1 says a seventh is a ruling. It is also the aspect with the least falsifiable data, which collides with section 7's rule that memory stays anchored to external facts - an aspect whose only input is conversation is a model reasoning about a man's life from memory. Schoolwork cannot be advised on because Canvas still has no sync; today's fix let the phone SEE assignments, it did not make them current. And "what needs doing" is scattered across checklists, list_items and TASK rows with nothing asking all three at once - which is the cheapest real step here and needs no ruling at all. Overdue tasks are KEPT rather than hidden, in their own section - a deadline that slid is still work, and dropping it quietly is the same class of lie as rendering a failed read as an empty day; bounded to 14 days back, since a deadline from five weeks ago is history. Tomorrow's nine are grouped by course, because the course is the only thing separating them at a glance. And the count is stated in words - "9 things due tomorrow, 1 already done" - rather than left to be derived by counting rows. Stale is a third sentence, and it did not exist. Empty and unreachable were both built; TanStack Query serves the last good response when a refetch fails and isError stays false while cached data exists, so a day view could be hours old and say nothing. Two columns from lg up - the day on the left, the strip and what is due after tomorrow on the right - with max-w-6xl as a ceiling rather than a corset. The phone keeps its single column. /api/changes dropped every aspect but the last, so the calendar was always empty
no ticket
52b28c0 · 4 files
Kevin's Today screen said "Nothing on the calendar today" while the database held 467 events. It said it every day. `aspects` is declared in openapi.yaml as `type: array` with no style/explode. OpenAPI's default for a query array is explode: true - repeated params, `?aspects=events&aspects=checklists`. The generated TypeScript client sent exactly that. This endpoint read `query_params.get("aspects")`, which returns only the LAST occurrence, so a client obeying the published contract asked for events and checklists and received `["checklists"]`. The server was wrong, not the client. The spec said repeated; the implementation only ever read comma-separated. It failed silently and in the worst direction: a 200 with no `events` key, which renders as "nothing on the calendar" and is indistinguishable from a household that genuinely has nothing on. Checklists worked the whole time, which is what made it look like a calendar problem rather than a query-string problem. Fixed by accepting BOTH rather than narrowing the spec and regenerating clients: getlist picks up every repeated occurrence and each is still comma-split, so the documented form keeps working and mixed spellings work too. Found by querying the API by hand from the browser once the screen and the data disagreed. Three wrong guesses came first and each was discarded on evidence: I grepped the built CSS for "min-width: 768px" and called a missing breakpoint the bug (Tailwind v4 emits "@media (width>=48rem)" - the responsive rules were complete); I suspected the day bucketing (the app's own arithmetic put the row on today correctly); and I suspected the service worker again (the new build was loading). The query string was the last difference left. 13 tests in test_changes_api.py. The new one pins the repeated form, the comma form, and the two mixed - a contract mismatch that returns a cheerful 200 is worse than one that 400s. The service worker waited for every tab to close, so deploys looked like no-ops
no ticket
206af39 · 3 files
Kevin, on his phone after the Today/Lists deploy: "i still see the same layout. not the mobile version." registerType: 'autoUpdate' installs a new worker but, on its own, leaves it in `waiting` until the last client holding the OLD one goes away. A PWA on a home screen or a tab left open can hold it for days. Nothing errors - the app just keeps serving the previous build, so a deploy looks like it did nothing. This is the second time today: the login screen was still reading "Not connected yet" from a build two days old, and I told him to clear the cache by hand rather than fixing it. skipWaiting + clientsClaim, verified present in the generated sw.js. Safe here because /api/ is NetworkOnly: taking over mid-session can swap the shell under a user, but it can never serve a cached figure, which is what CLAUDE.md section 4 actually cares about. The shell may be stale, the data may not. I was wrong twice on the way to this and both are worth recording. I first grepped the built CSS for "min-width: 768px", found nothing, and said I had found the bug - Tailwind v4 emits "@media (width>=48rem)", so the responsive rules were there all along. The md:flex / md:hidden / md:flex-row declarations are complete and correct. Grepping for a syntax the tool does not emit and reading the absence as a finding is how you invent a bug. read_calendar could not see a single assignment
canvas-integration 01one-today 01
9e53ac2 · 7 files
Kevin, 2026-09-11: "the AI doesnt see anything thats due on sunday for sch. i asked it and it didnt know." Seven were due that night. read_calendar queried EventKind.EVENT. Every assignment is EventKind.TASK. On the A25 that is 145 of 314 rows, and no tool in the toolbox returned one of them - read_list is reminders, manage_checklist is checklists, and NotesController.openAppointments is TASK-filtered but exists to match a spoken title for manage_item, not to read a day. Assignments were unreachable by voice entirely, which makes it an ADR 0035 gap as well: not a weak hands path, none. It failed in the worst available way. An empty window reads as "you have nothing due", which is indistinguishable from the truth. The first diagnosis was wrong and the ticket keeps it, because how it was wrong is the useful part. I had a timezone theory: Canvas writes an 11:59pm local deadline as 04:59Z the NEXT day, so every Sunday deadline carries a Monday UTC date, and this codebase has already been bitten by exactly that once (2026-09-01, "the due dates seem to be advanced by 1 day"). Plausible, and false. Pulling the Room database settled it in one query: allDay=0, a true instant, and activeByKindInLocalWindow was bucketing them onto the correct local day all along. The storage was never broken. I had also reached the right answer first and talked myself out of it, on two pieces of evidence that were both wrong. EventsBackend.kt:42 says of TASK "Nothing writes this yet" and NotesController.kt:929 repeats it - both stale, 145 rows exist. And APPOINTMENT was renamed to EVENT rather than TASK, which is true of the rename and false of the data. A stale comment is not ignored, it is believed. The fix: read both kinds, merged and sorted. Each row now reports kind, and done for a task, so the model can tell a class that passes from a quiz that is due and say whether it is already submitted. The description was wrong twice over and mattered more than it looks. Kevin, 2026-09-10: "we need to build the browser/mobile wrapper with household creation and user signup etc." His wife joins the existing household with a join code; his parents get a create-household code, which is the reason codes exist at all rather than one hardcoded household. The model - Invite: code, household (nullable), creates_household, created_by, max_uses, used_count, expires_at, revoked_at, created_at. Migration household/0003_invite.py, plus a CHECK constraint shipped by that migration - an invite either joins a household that exists or creates one, and CLAUDE.md section 7 puts an integrity rule that must hold when Django has a bug in SQL rather than in Python. - The code is twelve base64url characters from `secrets`, generated the way the ticket specifies. `Invite.mint()` returns it alongside the row, the same shape `DeviceToken.issue` uses, and `__str__` deliberately does not contain it so it cannot leak into an admin log or a traceback. It IS stored in the clear, unlike a device key, and the class docstring says why: an owner re-shares a live code and `/api/auth/invite/<code>` describes one before it is spent, and neither is possible against a hash. `Invite.find` compares with `secrets.compare_digest` after the indexed lookup - which changes no outcome under Postgres's byte-exact default collation, and is there because a credential comparison that rests on a collation setting is one nobody re-checks when the setting changes. The endpoints - POST /api/auth/signup. Validates the code, creates the user, joins or founds a household, issues a device token like login does, 201. Its own `signup` throttle scope at 5/min rather than sharing `login`, so a burst of signup attempts cannot lock the household out of signing in. The whole handler is one transaction and takes a row lock on the invite (`Invite.find(for_update=True)`), which is what makes max_uses real: without it two people redeeming the last use both read used_count before either writes. `for_update` drops the select_related, because Postgres refuses FOR UPDATE against the nullable side of an outer join and `household` is nullable here by design. - LEGION_OPEN_SIGNUP (settings, .env.example, off by default and no required_env - an operator who has not thought about it must get the closed behaviour). On, a request with no invite_code founds a household. A request that DOES carry a code is still honoured either way: the ticket's "always creates a household" is read as describing the codeless path, because the other reading leaves an open-signup engine unable to add a second adult to a household at all. - GET /api/auth/invite/<code>. Says whether a code is live, whether it joins or founds, and - only when it joins - the household's NAME, never its id. Spends nothing. Ticket 05's /join/<code> screen is the caller. Shares the `signup` throttle scope, so previewing and redeeming give a stranger five guesses a minute between them rather than five each. Unknown code 404s, a real-but-dead code answers 200 with live:false and a reason in words. - GET/PATCH /api/households/me, POST/GET/DELETE /api/households/me/invites, DELETE /api/households/me/members/<user_id>, in household/households.py under a new /api/households/ mount. GET is open to any member (a member who could not see the roster could not check they joined the right family); the other four are owner-only through a new IsHouseholdOwner, which guards exactly those membership verbs and no data route. - Removing a member revokes their live device tokens AND the invites they minted. The second is beyond the ticket's table and is the same failure one step removed: a removed person keeping a live code keeps a back door. Their User row survives with no household, so IsHouseholdMember refuses every request a surviving session makes. The last owner cannot be removed, themself included, and it refuses in words - a household with no owner has nobody who can ever invite or remove anyone again and no admin above it. - GET /api/auth/devices and DELETE /api/auth/devices/<id>: a member lists and revokes their OWN live tokens, never a key, and another person's token id 404s rather than 403s. - manage.py create_household --name --owner-email [--password] [--id], for the compose bootstrap path. Refuses to re-home somebody already in a household, and warns when the engine crosses from one household to two, because that is the moment add_household_member and the superuser signal stop being able to guess. No household field on /api/auth/me, and that is one row of the ticket's own table not built as written. tests/test_tenancy.py's test_no_openapi_component_declares_household_id forbids any component declaring `household` or `household_id`; it caught the first attempt this morning and 64004e7 reverted it. GET /api/households/me carries the household id because it IS the household resource, which is a different thing. The ticket body now says so where the table is. Three tests on Android CI's Linux runner asserted facts about the local SQLite/OS environment rather than about DatabaseSnapshot's own behaviour, so they passed on Kevin's Windows box and failed on Linux CI: - The VACUUM INTO spike asserted the call THROWS under Robolectric's bundled SQLite. It does on Windows, doesn't on Linux. Rewritten to record which answer the platform gives without asserting one; kept as a spike for its documentation value (it still runs the exact statement exportLocalCopy runs, and still checks the fast path produces a real file when it succeeds). - The fallback-branch test asserted CHECKPOINT_COPY was the method actually taken - which depended on the spike's throw. Rewritten to drive the fallback deterministically via a new forceFallback param on DatabaseSnapshot.exportLocalCopy (test-only seam, default false), so the test genuinely exercises the checkpoint+copy path - the thing that protects a real device too old for VACUUM INTO - on either OS. - The rollback test forced a failed renameTo by holding a file lock on the source file, relying on Windows's mandatory file locking; POSIX rename() doesn't consult open descriptors so this was a no-op on Linux and the rename silently succeeded. Replaced with DatabaseSnapshot.installRenameOverride, a test-only seam that forces the install rename to fail deterministically on any OS. Both seams are internal, default to production behaviour (null/false), and are documented in DatabaseSnapshot's own doc comments as test-only. No test was skipped, ignored, or weakened to reach green - each now proves the outcome it always claimed to (readable file, correct data, rollback on a failed install) without depending on which OS runs it. Two things Kevin asked for, and one live bug that fell out of building them. The wake word was "hey <companion name>". It is a fixed pair now: "excelsior" to wake, "that will be all" to end the conversation. WakePhrases owns both, and the first tests the wake grammar has ever had. The two halves are implemented differently because they have to be. MicArbiter grants the microphone to one claimant and LIVE_TURN outranks WAKE_WORD, so the instant a conversation starts, WakeWordEngine is preempted and releases capture. During the only window in which a sleep phrase means anything, Vosk is not listening at all, and a sleep entry in the grammar would have shipped as dead code that read like a feature. Sleep runs on the Live input transcript instead (where CrisisDetector already reads), through the model's end_conversation tool with a deterministic match behind it. Both arm one idempotent flag consumed at TurnComplete, so the sign-off is never cut off and the two paths cannot fight. "hey <name>" is retained behind the new phrase on purpose. The small Vosk model compiles its lexicon into binary FSTs, so there is no way to confirm off the device that "excelsior" is recognisable at all, and a grammar of only that word would listen forever for something nobody can say. Delete the second entry once the phone confirms it fires. switch_companion hands the conversation over by name. The voice and the persona clause are both baked into the socket's setup message with no way to patch them on an open socket, so a switch is a teardown and a fresh connect: the tool arms rather than fires, the outgoing companion says one handover line, and the incoming one greets on its own prompt. The resume handle is dropped deliberately, and HANDOVER_PROMPT tells the incoming companion it does not know what was said, so it cannot claim a continuity it does not have. Asking for a built-in with no profile row creates one from the persona's defaults, which is what makes "put Kratos on" work before Kratos has ever been created by hand. The bug: CompanionProfileStore.switchActive had no session-layer caller at all. Tapping a different companion on the Companions screen wrote the choice and stopped there, so AriaBrain's two-minute base-instruction cache and the warm socket both kept the previous companion, in the previous voice. Switching by hand changed the label and nothing audible. The car switch has had this wiring since 2026-07-16; the companion switch never did. Both doors now go through LiveSessionController.companionChanged, so the hands path gets the same spoken handover the voice path does. ADR 0046 and 0047. Kratos himself landed in 4bdf16a, swept into that commit by another session. Verified: compileDebugKotlin, detekt, and 3484 unit tests all green, read from the JUnit XML. Nothing here has run on the phone yet, and the one claim that only hardware can settle is whether "excelsior" fires at all. Then two ownership statements failed in turn - one because it tried to alter a table already owned correctly, one because Postgres 17 splits role membership into INHERIT and SET and postgres held admin on legion_engine with set=false, which ALTER TABLE OWNER TO requires. Granting SET fixed it and all 45 tables are legion_engine's now, which is the end state ADR 0044 wanted anyway: the role Django connects as owns the schema Django owns. Every failed attempt rolled back whole and was verified to have changed nothing. Two fresh pg_dump backups were taken first, both verified readable. An arm64 image that builds its own web bundle, and a deploy the box runs itself
web-and-households 08web-and-households 09
defa50b · 15 files
web-and-households ticket 09, and ticket 08's deferred CD half. server/Dockerfile becomes two stages. node:24-slim runs `npm ci` and `npm run build`; the python stage takes the bundle with COPY --from and runs collectstatic, so WhiteNoise's manifest storage hashes and compresses every file at image build time rather than on a running container. The one thing that was hardcoded to amd64 was the supercronic download, and the VM is Ampere. It is now keyed on TARGETARCH with a checksum per architecture. Both SHA1s were confirmed twice - the asset downloaded and hashed, and the value aptible publishes in the v0.2.49 release notes - and the amd64 one came back identical to the value this file already carried, which is what says the method used for the new arm64 one is sound. amd64 e63c11a9726b775a6a11801e81af4f3fb926aa68 (unchanged) arm64 0b6c5bb743e0b0dafed1132198c81807927ac413 (new) TARGETARCH is given a default because `gcloud builds submit` runs the classic builder, which never populates it, and Cloud Run is the thirty-day rollback. Three things here are correctness rather than tidiness, each found by looking rather than by reasoning: - server/.dockerignore excludes the developer's own static/app and staticfiles. Docker does not read .gitignore, so without it `COPY . .` lays down a stale local build first and COPY merges rather than replaces - collectstatic would then hash and ship a mix of two builds with nothing broken enough to notice. - collectstatic's five required_env variables are inline on that one RUN and not ENV. As ENV they would survive into the running container, and a household that forgot to set SECRET_KEY would silently inherit a throwaway one instead of the loud failure required_env exists to produce. - The Caddyfile's `email "{$LEGION_ACME_EMAIL}"` is quoted. Unquoted and empty, Caddy substitutes textually, sees a bare `email` token and refuses to start - measured with caddy validate, both ways. The entrypoint is server/entrypoint.sh, NOT deploy/entrypoint.sh as tickets 09 and 13 both say. It cannot live in deploy/: the build context is server/ in all three places that build this image - compose's web and worker, and deploy/cloudrun/deploy.py's `docker build server/` and `gcloud builds submit server/` - a COPY ../ is not expressible, and Cloud Build does not support BuildKit named contexts. The script says so at the top so ticket 13's runbook writer reads it before writing the wrong path. The image gains an ENTRYPOINT and loses its CMD. With an ENTRYPOINT set a CMD becomes arguments to it, so the Cloud Run service - which overrides neither - would have run the entrypoint with gunicorn's command line as argv. On the CD side the box builds its own image: arm64 native, no registry, no QEMU on an amd64 runner. deploy.sh pulls --ff-only (a diverged box is an operator problem, not something a deploy silently merges), brings compose up, then polls /health for 60s because web migrates before gunicorn binds and a single curl would fail every deploy that carried a migration. The workflow is one SSH call to a key whose authorized_keys entry is restricted with command=, so a leak buys one deploy of what is already on main. shellcheck earned its place: the specified `#!/bin/bash -euo pipefail` shebang is SC2096. Linux passes everything after the interpreter as one argument, so bash would have exited "invalid option" before reading a line. It is `set -euo pipefail` on line 2 instead. Verified without Docker, which this machine does not have: hadolint 2.15.1 clean, shellcheck 0.11.0 clean on both scripts, actionlint 1.7.12 clean on all four workflows, caddy 2.11.4 validate clean with the variables set and unset and fmt clean, compose YAML parsed with every service still carrying a profile and the worker's supercronic entrypoint override intact. THE IMAGE HAS NEVER BEEN BUILT, for either architecture. Ticket 09's "done means" is entirely unmet and owed on the first machine with Docker. deploy/.env.vm.example is a snippet, not a second env file: .env.example was being edited by another builder at the time. Its two variables need merging into .env.example and the file deleted. Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5.1 <noreply@anthropic.com> Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_0151LEjTxzhNdAtbjU4Rpw9m

A web client generated from the contract, and Django to serve it
web-and-households 04
788d222 · 39 files
web-and-households ticket 04, the scaffold Kevin's React + Vite + TypeScript decision describes. Nothing hand-writes an API shape: `src/api/schema.d.ts` is generated from `server/openapi.yaml` by `npm run gen:api`, and `npm run check:api` regenerates and diffs it, so a server rename becomes a build failure in the web app instead of a 404 someone finds later. Three things were found by running it rather than by reading about it, and each one is commented where it bites: - Every asset URL 404'd into the SPA shell. Vite's `base: '/'` makes the page ask for `/assets/index-<hash>.js`, Django serves static under `/static/`, so the catch-all answered `200 text/html` for a script request - measured, 1226 bytes of HTML where the bundle should be. `WHITENOISE_ROOT` is the fix. - WhiteNoise ignores Python's `mimetypes` and carries its own table with no `.webmanifest` entry, so the manifest went out as `application/octet-stream` and the browser would silently decline to offer "install". A first attempt through `mimetypes.add_type()` changed nothing, which is how the private table came to light; `WHITENOISE_MIMETYPES` is what actually works. - `openapi-fetch` reads `globalThis.fetch` once, when `createClient` runs. A test double installed after that instant is ignored - one test's mock was still serving the next test. The client passes a thunk so the lookup happens per call. The README's `uv sync` line is corrected in passing: `pyproject.toml` has no `[project]` table, so `uv lock` refuses and `uv sync` syncs to an EMPTY set - against a working venv it uninstalls Django and everything else. It did, here. `uv pip install -r requirements.txt` is what actually reads the pins. `/login` is a form shell with a disabled button that says so in words. There is no browser session endpoint until ticket 03, and a form that looks live but cannot sign anyone in is a claim the app has not earned. Verified on the dev server: `/` serves the shell with `Cache-Control: no-store`, `/api/auth/me` answers 401 JSON, `/health` answers `{"db":"ok"}`, `/does-not-exist` serves the shell, `/admin/` still redirects to Django's login. With the bundle absent, `/` is a 503 in words, never a stack trace. Vitest 2/2, `tsc -b` clean, `manage.py check` clean, the contract byte-identical. BodyWriteThrough and MemoryWriteThrough inserted into Room unconditionally and pushed afterwards, so a row Django would refuse was accepted locally, the user was told it was logged, and the drain then retried three times and poisoned it. Deletes stay local-first on both transports, because a 4xx on a delete is routinely a 404 for a row the engine never had, and refusing to tombstone locally would make a phone-only row undeletable. The section 4 gate moves language, not posture

django-engine ticket 03. ADR 0044 decision 2 rules it plainly - "the gate moves language, not posture; rules 1 to 8 bind the Python implementation exactly as they bound the plpgsql" - and decision 1 names the four things that stay in SQL, of which the gate is not one. I briefed the opposite from ADR 0042's body without reading its Standing banner, which 0044 amends away; the builder refused the brief, cited both files, and was right. The argument that actually settles it is simpler than the doctrine: a gate left in plpgsql has no owner once supabase/migrations stops being the migration directory. ingest/gate.py is pure - no ORM, no Django import - and every branch quotes the SQL line it mirrors. dedup.py ports the two-pass depleting credit pool. POST /api/ingest/statement and /receipt return the RPC's own verdict, plus the anchors echoed (rule 8) and the estimates named in words (rule 5). Rule 5 is enforced by shape rather than discipline: check_receipt cannot see the macros at all. The corpus is a THIRD READER of app/src/test/resources/gate-corpus.json, not a copy - all 17 cases run twice, pure and over HTTP, with the payload mapping taken from the SQL runner so both sides send the same request. Rule 8 audited against the live schema, not the migrations: both paths already store every anchor, nothing missing, no migration owed. The sharp half is pinned - an unprinted tax is stored NULL, never the zero the arithmetic used to add up. Rule 7 turned out not to be a property of these endpoints at all: three CHECK constraints forbid a provisional row from reaching either commit path, so the honest answer to a no-anchor document is a quarantine with wording, and that is what is tested. no ticket

My partial index broke the fix it was part of. PostgREST sends a bare ON CONFLICT (client_uuid) and Postgres cannot infer a partial index from it, so every audit upload batch was rejected outright and the 142 stranded rows moved nowhere. The predicate was pointless anyway - a plain unique index already permits many NULLs, because Postgres treats them as distinct. I engineered an exemption that was the default. 7dffc04 · 6 files
Ticket 09 decision 4: a list with no schedule appears every day and its lines are done once - a tick on any day counts. A DAILY or WEEKLY list is tracked per day. The controller keyed that choice on recursDaily, which the new schedule picker never writes, so every list created through the UI was silently per-day and "done once, ever" was unreachable. It now derives the mode from scheduleKind: null is any-day, non-null is per-day. recursDaily is read nowhere in the controller and its doc says it is migration-only. Kevin's bio list is unchanged - v66 backfilled it to DAILY from recursDaily = 1, traced in the migration rather than assumed. itemsWithTickState also gains its own failure signal, Loaded or Failed, the same shape VoiceNoteController.listInRange uses, so the calendar's collapsed header can say "couldn't load" from a real result instead of a catch around the call. One thing the Failed test taught: corrupting the database file does NOT make Room throw. Android's SQLiteDatabase detects corruption on open and quietly deletes and recreates an empty database, so the read came back as a clean empty Loaded. The test closes the live cached instance instead, which cancels Room's scope and makes the next DAO call throw for real. Both approaches are written down in the test so the next person does not rediscover the first. 3055 -> 3060 tests, 0 failures. The controller's own doc comment said it outright: "there is no separate 'processing failed' flag to set." Written down, in the file, and shipped anyway. A spinner that can only be left by succeeding is the app asserting an outcome it never observed - §7's rule, which everyone reads as being about what the assistant SAYS, applied to what a screen shows. Nobody thought of a spinner as a sentence. So: a FAILED state, checked before TRANSCRIBING so a failed row can never read as in-flight, and the REASON stored rather than a boolean. §4 rule 8's posture - a verdict with no retrievable evidence is unactionable - and ListItem.exactDowngraded is the precedent for storing the words of a refusal rather than only the fact of one. One real race fixed on the way: the failure write used dao.update() with a snapshot taken before the network call, so a rename landing in between was silently reverted. A tick is a row with a day on it
one-today 09
282a596 · 18 files
Kevin wants a list he names himself - bio, with "3 sets goblet squats" under it - optionally daily, ticked as he goes, and browsable afterwards. He described it as recording and resetting at end of day. The reset is not built, deliberately. Every daily mechanism in this app is app-open-triggered or an AlarmManager shot at an instant; there is no WorkManager dependency and ScheduledBackup records that as a ruling. A midnight sweep is the part that rots - phone off at midnight, a timezone change, three days unopened, the job running twice and double-recording. So a tick is a row keyed by (item, day) and nothing sweeps. Tomorrow queries tomorrow, finds nothing, and shows everything unticked; the reset falls out for free. History is that same query against a past day. A missed day reads as missed because no row was written, not because a job decided so. day and tickedAt are stored separately on purpose. day is which day the tick counts for, tickedAt is when the finger actually moved. They diverge the moment you tick yesterday this morning, and collapsing them would make a retroactive tick indistinguishable from a real-time one. One tick model, not two: a non-recurring list uses the same rows and is done when a tick exists on any day. A done boolean would have been simpler and would have thrown away when each line happened. Both history-lying traps are closed in the controller rather than in a screen, so no future UI can reopen them. A day before the checklist existed returns empty, not a wall of things you failed to do - gated on createdAt compared as a local day, never as a raw timestamp. And items soft-delete without cascading their ticks, so dropping goblet squats next month leaves last week still saying you did them; the history read resolves text for deleted items precisely so it can. One thing the brief missed and a test caught: an untick soft-deletes the tick, which still occupies the unique (item, day) slot, so INSERT OR IGNORE would have silently swallowed the re-tick. It revives the tombstone with a fresh tickedAt instead. Maintenance is NOT joining this, though Kevin named it. Ticket 05 traces why: due-ness is derived at read time from service_records on a miles-or-months anchor, and the server schema carries no last-done columns at all by design. There is no day an oil change belongs to. v63 -> v64, three new tables, SQL verbatim from the generated 64.json. 2999 -> 3015 tests, 0 failures. UI is the next slice. One live join site, confirmed by tracing rather than assuming - FleetRecordBridge.toMaintenanceItem turns out to have zero callers, and FleetEngineStore.get's exact-name lookup is a different thing on purpose. never_done defaulted false in Room and true in Supabase, and isDue's first line is "if (neverDone) return true" - so the default decided whether an unanchored item read as always-overdue or as unknown. False is right: an item with no history is unknown, which is what isUnknown exists to say, and true would have made all 54 claim to be due at once. The migration sets the server default to false and carries NO update. There is no upsert for maintenance_schedules on FleetBackend at all - the fleet cutover never built one - so nothing in this repo has ever written that table. That also means this was a trap for whoever builds that sync, not a live bug, and it is now disarmed before the sync exists rather than after. Suite 2853, 0 failures. So: a web app, one responsive codebase, is the GENERAL client - wide viewport gets ingest and monitor, narrow gets calendar, todos, lists, notes, on any phone, added to the Home Screen, no Apple developer account. LEGION becomes the SPECIALIZED client: OBD, wake word, background audio, Alfred - the things a browser cannot reach. That is a much sharper reason for the Android app to exist. 'The phone client' invites every feature to be built twice; 'the client for what needs hardware a browser cannot touch' does not. Kevin's framing for the whole system is Lattice - one central database, many things connecting to it - and it decides something concrete: capability lives in the data layer, not in a client. N clients over one record must not each reimplement the rules or they will disagree, and the disagreement surfaces months later as a wrong number. This project already did that once without naming it: the gate lives in SQL and every client inherits it. Repeat the pattern, do not treat it as a special case. The limit is written down too, because that analogy invites over-building: Lattice is a product with a company; this is two adults, two phones and a laptop. The useful part is the shape, not the scale. No platform, no abstraction for clients that do not exist. Ticket 23 opened for the second account. The server side turns out to be a dashboard task - ticket 02 designed for exactly this - so what it really owes is proving household RLS shows her the same rows, and one deliberate pass over the policies before a public URL makes RLS internet-reachable rather than theoretical. Also recorded: iOS push works only from the Home Screen and less reliably than native. Reminders that must FIRE are the one capability where the web app's ceiling is lower and the difference is silent - test it early rather than assume it. Make the suite green on purpose instead of by luck
hardening 13
9ae71c9 · 86 files
Six test classes leaked "Illegal connection pointer" out of Room's invalidation tracker onto an arch_disk_io thread, uncaught, and kotlinx-coroutines-test blamed whichever runTest started next. Which test died depended on execution order, so any change moved the casualty and every fix looked like it worked. Option 2 (synchronous disk IO) was disqualified on evidence: Room's assertNotMainThread checks Looper directly, not ArchTaskExecutor, and two tests already need allowMainThreadQueries because Robolectric's test thread IS the main-looper thread. It would have broken the 79-file surface that relies on hopping off that thread. The fix is a pool-quiescence barrier using only java.util.concurrent and ArchTaskExecutor's public Executor: submit one barrier task per pool thread, and the instant all are parked together, everything queued before them is provably done. No Room internals, no changed execution semantics for the rest of the suite. The first placement was wrong and a real run said so. Draining in @Before still leaked, because Robolectric resets its shadow layer for method M before any of M+1 runs. The drain has to happen inside the causing test's own lifecycle, so it moved to @After across 78 files, plus two that build their own in-memory database and never touched the singleton. Bounded waits, added on review. A stale pool-size constant fails two ways: a grown pool under-drains and the leak returns looking like the original bug; a shrunk pool could never trip the barrier. Unbounded, the second case would HANG the suite - no report, no failing test name, and on CI the whole time budget burned before anyone learns anything. It now fails with an error naming the constant to fix. Verified across five clean full runs, test-results deleted each time: 2,744 tests, 0 failures, and 0 classes emitting the leak in system-err. The leak count is the assertion that matters. A green suite that still leaked would mean the casualty moved, not that the cause was fixed - which is exactly how this survived being waved off as a flake, by me, twice today. IngestScanner stores the stripped id at :183 and opens bytes with the full child.documentId at :192, so the live scan never round-trips through the stored form. The dry run did, handing a stripped id to buildDocumentUriUsingTree and producing a document id Drive does not recognise. Real values off the phone: stored doc=encoded=9SUKrD9cnjOCA5TdkI8TKpsIuHE3q5gJ... tree URI acc=1;doc=encoded=o_GGpalKBAfTlOkt93tJoIsI7YFN... reattachAccountPrefix is the documented inverse, sitting next to its counterpart so neither gets "simplified" without the other. The prefix is derived from the tree's own document id rather than stored, so a non-Drive provider that carries no prefix gets nothing fabricated, and an already-prefixed id is not double-prefixed. Both cases tested. The regression test asserts on the URI that gets built, and separately asserts the old direct-build path produces a different, wrong id - so it fails if the fix regresses rather than only if a read throws. ## How it got through, which is the part worth keeping The claim was "grepped the whole repo for the literal acc=, found zero producers of that prefix", tagged traced. True and irrelevant: the prefix is produced by Drive, not by this codebase, and the existence of stripAccountPrefix - a consumer that removes it - is itself proof the input carries it. Evidence gathered in the wrong direction and then labelled verified. The claim never landed in a comment or a ticket, so there was nothing in-repo to correct, but the shape is worth naming: an absence of producers inside one repo says nothing about what an external provider hands you. The three-anchor CSV format, and a parse that refuses to be helpful
no ticket
ed5d7c5 · 7 files
Hard constraint C4: the format and its importer must work before the ledger cutover, and only then do the deterministic parsers come out. Neither existed. The server half was already done and proven - the RPC is applied and the 13-case corpus reports both implementations agree - so this is the format itself and the phone side that produces its payload. ## The format is a contract with the user's own LLM Not with a bank. That inverts the usual design pressure: it has to be simple enough that a person can describe it in a paragraph and an arbitrary model hits it first try. So it is two plain CSV tables, an anchor header and one row, then the lines, and there is deliberately NO quoting support - a quoting rule is one more thing for a model to get subtly wrong. Money is a bare signed integer of cents. No dollar sign, no commas, no decimal point, and anything else is REJECTED rather than coerced. That refusal is the point. The gate proves three printed numbers agree with each other; it cannot prove any one of them was read correctly, so a parser that helpfully strips a "$" is exactly how a misread digit enters the one place nothing downstream can catch it. Every cents field goes through a single regex or fails - no strip, no replace, no repair. Rows are tagged LLM_RECONCILED, never DETERMINISTIC. LEGION's own parse IS deterministic, but an LLM sat upstream, and provenance describes where data came from rather than what last touched it. A statement missing any one anchor cannot use the format at all and fails early, naming which anchor was absent. It falls to rule 7 provisional instead, which is where an unverifiable row belongs. ## The corpus now proves the real code path, not a lookalike The gate arithmetic came out into LedgerReconciliationCheck, one pure function mirroring commit_statement's SQL check for check and wording for wording. GateCorpusTest was reimplementing that arithmetic inline; it now calls the production function, so the corpus's own promise - "when the pre-check lands, plug in here" - is literally true. Kotlin production code, the corpus and the RPC agree by construction rather than by three hand-copied copies of one rule. That is better than the extra corpus cases I asked for, which would have padded coverage of shapes already covered while leaving the real function unproven. Recorded because the agent flagged the deviation rather than quietly taking it. The existing parsers are untouched and still dispatch. Widen the Google importer, so the metadata outlives Google
no ticket
6e36ef1 · 13 files
Hard constraint C3 from the migration path: widen the importer, run it unbounded, verify, and only THEN remove Google. The reason the order binds is that the class-schedule metadata lives ONLY in Google's event descriptions and is never stored, so cutting first deletes it for good. The importer handled none of description, location, allDay or the LEGION::v1 block, so nothing was ready to cut against. Now it does. description and location land in the existing engine fields, allDay and structuredMeta are new field defs (a FieldDef row, the engine's own zero-migration extension mechanism, not invented storage), and proseAfter is the counterpart to structuredBlock: the human-written text after the terminator, null and never "" when there is nothing to say - an empty string would later read as "the user wrote nothing", which is a claim the source never made. ## Unbounded is a different mode, not a wider window The windowed run's delete guard exists because a windowed query is narrower than what a differently-windowed prior run could have written, so an out-of-window row is not "gone from Google", merely out of scope. An unbounded run has no such gap: every google row is in scope by construction, so a row not re-seen really is gone. Reusing the guard would be reusing semantics built around a gap that does not exist. Added as a mode rather than a changed default, and the difference is tested both ways. Read in year-wide slices rather than one span, because CalendarProvider materializes a plain List with no paging contract. A multi-day event straddling a slice boundary is handled by writing new ids into the shared map immediately, so the second sighting updates rather than duplicates. ## The fields did not actually survive the trip, and that is the point Caught on review, after the work already looked complete and green: EventsReconcile hardcoded allDay = false for Dates events - it never read a field because Dates had no such field until this commit. So an all-day event imported true and uploaded false. Silent loss on the exact field just added, now read properly and asserted. structuredMeta reached nothing at all: no column, no DTO. The metadata rescued out of Google's description strings would have lived only in an engine field, and ruling 7 retires the engine. That defers the loss C3 exists to prevent rather than preventing it. Added structured_meta jsonb on public.events and carried it end to end. jsonb over text because a text blob is the "enforcement caps at whatever the client remembers" shape ruling 6 rejected. And the DTO carries it as JsonElement, not String: a String property serializes to Postgrest as a quoted JSON scalar, writing the whole object as one escaped string and destroying the indexability that was the reason for jsonb at all. Same fix SupabasePantryBackend already uses for the identical problem. EventReplica deliberately gets NO column and there is no v43. Nothing on the phone renders a LEGION::v1 block - the only live consumer reads straight off a Google description - so a Room migration would buy an unread column. The reasoning is on toReplica's doc comment so it is not silently "fixed" later without re-checking. Suite: 2,701 tests, 0 failures. 20260827000100 is NOT APPLIED. No CLI or credentials here, same as 54cdf5e. Owed with the fleet migrations. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

The agenda shows an undated item as tomorrow, and says so in words

Ticket 01 ruling 2 has been decided since 2026-08-25 and nothing implemented it. Both agenda queries hard-filtered dueAt IS NOT NULL and toAgendaItems dropped null rows, so 53 of Kevin's 56 Notes items - 95% of everything he has authored in this aspect - never reached the agenda at all. That is a bug against the ruling, not a missing feature. All five clauses of the ruling, each load-bearing: INFERRED, never stored. Nothing is written; the date is synthesized per read. Storage keeps NULL, per ticket 07's own "what it does not license" and section 4 rule 5. TAGGED. AgendaItem.dueIsInferred is an explicit flag, not a sentinel date, so no caller has to infer the inference. SAID IN WORDS. An inferred item renders as "(showing tomorrow, no date set)", never a bare time that reads as stated. The spoken opener carries it too - clause 3 applies to speech, not just to a screen. ROLLS FORWARD. Computed from a nowMs parameter on every read and never cached, so it is always ahead and can never become yesterday. The parameter exists so tests can pin it rather than race the clock. NEVER NAGS, and this is the safety-relevant one. An inferred date must never fire an alarm: that would be the app asserting a deadline the user never set, which is rule 5 and fails the compulsion test's clause (a), since the anchor would not be a fact he could verify. The asymmetry is what makes that real - visible on the agenda, invisible to the alarm scheduler - and it is enforced STRUCTURALLY rather than by a filter. Inferred rows come from a separate DAO method that only windowed() calls; nextUnmuted and byId keep their untouched dueAt IS NOT NULL query and null guard, so an inferred row cannot reach the alarm path even if a future caller forgets it exists. A widened query with an OR would have made "never nags" depend on every caller remembering to filter it back out. The inferred instant is now + 24h rather than a calendar midnight. Accepted as a judgment call, not dictated by the ruling: it needs no timezone and is always ahead of now. Adding 24h lands on calendar tomorrow in every case except a near-midnight DST spring-forward, and since the rendered text never shows the date, the only thing affected is sort position. Six new tests, including the one that matters: an inferred row is excluded from nextUnmuted even when it would otherwise sort soonest. Suite: 2,676 tests, 0 failures. Derive the replica's local id instead of reminting it every reconcile
backend-erp 11
b17bc88 · 5 files
Ticket 11 grounding found a live defect, not a hazard to be careful of during the rewire. EventsReconcile.run deletes every replica row before refilling it, so EventReplicaDao.upsert's getByServerId branch always missed, every row took the insert path, and EVERY local id was reminted on EVERY reconcile. The hand-written id-preserving upsert was defeated by its only production caller; its doc comment described a guarantee the code did not deliver. That id is load-bearing: it is an AlarmManager PendingIntent request code, a notification id, and a soft foreign key from list_item_skips, workout_set_logs and muted_reminders. A reminted id orphans an armed alarm that can then never be cancelled, while the real one is silently dropped. Kevin's ruling: carry the engine id. events_replica.id is now DERIVED from the originating records.id via origin_guid rather than allocated by SQLite. A derived id cannot drift, so the defect dissolves rather than getting patched, and the cutover needs no rekey and no alarm re-arm. Two-pass refill, and the ordering is load-bearing. Rows with a derivable id are seated BEFORE any id is allocated. Without that, an ancestor-less row (created post-cutover on another surface, no origin_guid) refilling into the just-emptied table autoincrements from 1 and can take the very id a not-yet-processed migrated row must carry; the collision guard then correctly declines to clobber it and hands the migrated row a fresh id, which is the alarm orphaning the carry exists to prevent, reached by another route. An ancestor-less row has nothing pointing at its local id yet, so it is the one that can afford to move. upsert keeps three branches: an established id never moves, not even to a more correct carried one; an unoccupied carried id is honoured; else autoincrement. The collision guard stays as defence for callers other than the reconcile. Why no test caught it: the idempotence test asserted replicaCountAfter, never ids. Ticket 09's blind spot one layer out, and section 4 rule 6's shape - a check satisfiable without the thing it protects being present. The new stability test was confirmed RED against the unfixed code. Suite: 2,656 tests, 0 failures. compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey clean. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Phase 3: the read-state vocabulary, and a correction to what phase 3 is for
backend-erp 05
bea1cef · 4 files
ReadState is the pure, Compose-free piece: what a screen knows about its own last read, and the words it owes because of it. Nine tests, no Robolectric, following TodayGapResolvers, which is the in-house precedent for a builder that returns already-worded strings plus a severity flag so the composable picks a colour rather than re-deriving meaning from the string it is about to print. Kevin's two rulings are encoded in it. Fresh data says nothing, because a permanent "as of just now" trains the eye past exactly the line that matters once reads go remote. And a failure keeps the last good data on screen and says so, rather than blanking working figures over a transient blip. Ordering inside readStateLine is the design: a failure with no data ever loaded is worded differently from a failure with data, because "showing the last data read" would be a lie when there is nothing on screen; and a failure outranks staleness, since the age of the last successful read is misleading on its own. The staleness rule ships with tests but no live trigger, deliberately. Reads are still local and complete in milliseconds, so the app cannot reach it until phase 4. Shipping it tested-but-unreached is the considered alternative to shipping an untested half, which is exactly what the DatabaseSnapshot restore turned out to be on the one path nobody had run. Also corrects a claim I put in this ticket myself. I wrote that the three screens "have no loading state, so an empty screen and a not-yet-loaded screen are the same pixels", from a summary I did not check. All three already have loading booleans and screen-level indicators, and FleetUiState.odometerUnset even defaults to true so a not-yet-loaded state cannot open the miles axis. What is actually missing is narrower and worse: there is no error channel at all, no try/catch in any of the three load effects, so a Room or bundled-asset throw crashes rather than surfacing. Plus the ledger money tiles conflate "this month is reloading" with "no data", pantry has no reload path whatsoever, no screen records when its load completed, and none of the three has any screenshot coverage. And the two "as of" facts are separated in writing so nobody merges them later: AccountBalance.asOfMs is the statement document's date, ruling 9's is when this device last read its copy, and both can be true at once. The cases that matter are the ones a careless corpus omits. An empty extraction whose stated figures are all zero satisfies every anchor on nothing at all. Phase 2: the shared gate corpus, ticket 03 ruling 2's actual deliverable
no ticket
1f7daa6 · 5 files
Ruling 2 accepted two implementations of the reconciliation arithmetic, a Kotlin pre-check and the SQL in the commit RPCs, on one condition: that something proves they agree. Nothing did. This is that something. gate-corpus.json is the single source of truth for what the gate must do, and both sides read the same file rather than being compared to each other. Each case states its own arithmetic in prose so a reader can check the expectation by hand. Thirteen cases. The ones that matter most are the ones a careless corpus would omit: an empty extraction whose stated figures are all zero, which satisfies every anchor on nothing at all and is exactly how a card statement once passed with four dropped interest rows; a statement whose lines sum to the printed total but whose balances disagree, which a single-anchor gate waves through and which is why ruling 4 demands three printed figures; a genuinely zero-movement month with real lines, guarding against over-correcting rule 6 into refusing legitimate zero sums; both halves of pantry's no-subtotal collapse, since a bug that always accepted that branch would pass a corpus containing only the happy half; and absurd macro estimates that must not affect a thing, because a receipt never prints calories. Two meta-tests guard the corpus itself. One fails if either aspect stops exercising both outcomes, because an all-COMMITTED corpus passes against a gate that never refuses and an all-QUARANTINED one passes against a gate that never accepts. The other fails if nobody keeps a case of the specific self-satisfying zero shape rule 6 exists for. The Kotlin side is honest about what it can assert today: the phone's pre-check does not exist yet, since ruling 3 retires the parsers for a CSV path that is unbuilt, so there is no gate function to call. What it checks is that every case follows from its own numbers, which makes the corpus self-verifying and is the same arithmetic the SQL implements. When the pre-check lands it plugs into the same corpus and the comparison becomes direct. gate_corpus.sql is generated and committed, following this repo's existing pattern for adr-index.md and Board.md, because there is no local Postgres and it has to be pasted into the editor to run. Phase 2: the real ledger dedup, and a schema bug it exposed
no ticket
07f77f3 · 3 files
Replaces the placeholder tuple match with a faithful port of LedgerDedup.resolveDedup: two passes over a shared, depleting credit pool. Exact strict-key matches first with no window condition, then loose matches with the description dropped, permitted only inside dates another committed statement already enumerated completely. Transcribed as a loop rather than expressed as an anti-join. A set-based version is derivable but only provably equivalent after working the arithmetic; a faithful loop that is obviously right beats a clever join that is probably right when the question is whether money gets counted twice. Three properties are load-bearing and each has a Kotlin test pinning it. Pass one runs completely before pass two, so a row that can be matched precisely never spends a loose credit another row needs. Both passes decrement the same pool, so one committed row absorbs exactly one incoming row and never two. And incoming is never deduplicated against itself, because two identical lines in one statement are two genuine purchases; collapsing them is the original bug the function exists to fix. The port exposed a real problem in my own schema rather than in the Kotlin. LedgerAccountIdentity is emphatic that sameCard's last-four suffix match must never be folded into the dedup key, since a checking account ending in the same four digits would absorb a card's rows. Ticket 03 ruling 5 then made the stored identity last-four plus nickname, so keying dedup on account_last4 alone would have reintroduced exactly that bug through the schema instead of the predicate. The key is now the pair, which restores plain equality on a full identity. The nickname is load-bearing, not a label. Windows derive their bounds from the actual first and last transaction dates rather than the printed period, because a printed period can run past the last transaction and claiming completeness over that tail would be unsupported. Derived rather than stored so it cannot drift from the rows. One accepted divergence is documented in place: Kotlin's uppercase is Locale.ROOT with full Unicode mapping, Postgres upper is collation-driven and does not expand one-to-many. For ASCII bank descriptions it never bites, and the failure direction is known - a divergence causes a false non-match, which double-counts. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Phase 2: the commit RPC, with the gate and rule 7 in one transaction
no ticket
39a44c3 · 2 files
The reconciliation gate, server side. Everything IngestPipeline.commit does inside one db.withTransaction now happens inside one PostgREST request, which is one Postgres transaction. One deliberate deviation from ticket 03's literal wording, stated at the top of the file rather than buried. The ticket says the RPC raises on a gate mismatch. Taken literally that is wrong: a raise rolls back everything including the quarantine record, so the file would return on the next scan with no memory of why it failed, forever. A gate failure is an outcome, not an exception, and the Kotlin version already treats it that way. It returns QUARANTINED having written exactly one file-status row and zero lines, which is what "nothing partial is ever written" actually prohibits: partial DATA, never the record that a document was rejected. Raise is reserved for genuinely exceptional states. Rule 6 runs FIRST, before any arithmetic, and the ordering is the point. A zero-line extraction sails through every anchor whenever the statement's own figures happen to be zero, because the sum of no rows is zero and a month with no movement has closing equal to opening. That is not hypothetical; it is how BofA's card statement passed with four silently dropped interest rows, and it only held because interest was zero that month. Rule 7 supersession runs before the dedup read, carrying all three load-bearing properties: a provisional file never supersedes anything including a prior import of itself, the ordering stops verified rows being discarded as duplicates of the provisional ones they replace, and it is in the same transaction by construction. sameCard becomes the last-four match, and its collision weakness carries over unchanged, which is what the nickname is for. Idempotency is keyed on the content hash, so a repeat call returns ALREADY_COMMITTED having written nothing. That is what lets the phone retry a lost ack instead of narrating a state CANNOT_CLAUSE has no vocabulary for. Dedup is deliberately incomplete rather than quietly partial: the tuple match is implemented, the overlapping-window restatement pass that distinguishes a real duplicate from a bank restating a period is not, and the comment says so and says it is owed before the phase 4 ledger cutover. The intra-file behaviour is also spelled out rather than left to be discovered. Not verified: no Postgres has run any of this. pglast parses the statements but plpgsql bodies are opaque to it, so every function body here is unproven. Ten tables across three migrations, 58 statements, all parsing against Postgres's own grammar. The gate's claim is that a set of lines reconciles against something the document stated, so making the anchor a header row the lines reference means a line cannot exist without the anchor it was checked against. "Nothing partial is ever written" stops being a property the commit code remembers and becomes one the database will not allow to be violated. Two constraints encode rule 7 rather than describing it. statements requires all three anchors NOT NULL, because a document that cannot state them cannot use the format at all. And ledger_transactions.statement_id is nullable precisely so a provisional row can exist without a header, with a CHECK tying the two together: reconciled rows must have one, provisional rows must not. The schema says in the only language it has that a provisional row was never checked against anything. Reversal columns carry the SAP document principle, and there is deliberately no reversed_by anywhere, because setting one would mean updating an immutable row. The Notes-into-Dates merge lands as one events table. Twenty-one Item fields and seven Event fields become one shape with nothing dropped, and event_skips carries over list_item_skips for the reason it existed before: occurrences are computed from the recurrence rule and never stored, so a skip has nowhere else to live. This is the only aspect with no legacy table to retreat to, which is why the merge happens here rather than twice. Fleet is where ADR 0039 pays for itself most visibly. "You may not delete a vehicle that still has service history" was a rule RecordStore enforced in Kotlin on every caller's behalf; it is now ON DELETE RESTRICT, which no future consumer can route around. Phase 2: schema conventions, and a parser so the SQL is not written blind
no ticket
71e42b2 · 3 files
The shared vocabulary every aspect table will follow: the provenance type, the immutability rule for gated data, updated_at for authored data, the household RLS macro, and the server-side ingested_files whose content hash is the commit RPC's idempotency key. Two design points are worth reading rather than skimming. Immutability and rule 7 appeared to collide: gated rows are append-only, but rule 7 deletes superseded provisional rows. The resolution is principled rather than a carve-out. Immutability protects rows asserted as FACT, and rule 7's own definition of a provisional row is that it is never asserted as fact and is transient. A row that was never a claim cannot be falsified by withdrawing it. So the trigger blocks every update, and blocks deletes except on UNRECONCILED. Freezing provisional rows instead would stop rule 7 running at all. There is deliberately no reversed_by column. Setting one would require updating an immutable row, which is the thing being forbidden. A reversal carries reversal_of, and "is this reversed" is a lookup rather than stored state. The RLS macro grants table privileges explicitly rather than leaning on Supabase's project defaults. If those defaults were ever altered, the tables would be unreadable and RLS would look like the culprit. tools/sql_check.py parses every migration through pglast, which wraps libpg_query, Postgres's own grammar. This matters because nothing on this machine can run Postgres: no psql, no Docker. Both migrations parse, 25 statements. Its docstring is explicit about what it cannot catch, because a check that overstates itself is worse than none: plpgsql function bodies are opaque string literals to the outer grammar and are only parsed by Postgres at execution, and nothing semantic is verified. Green means well formed, never "will apply". Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

ScheduledBackup follows CalendarImportController's shape per Kevin's call: an app-lifecycle daily check, no WorkManager, called from MainActivity.onResume under the same runCatching discipline as the hooks beside it. runIfDue takes an injected clock so the 24h boundary is testable without sleeping, and injected seams for SyncCapability and backupNow because neither is reachable from a JVM test. It never passes overrideGuard, since an unattended pass has nobody to ask for the confirmation DatabaseSnapshotGuard exists to demand. Six tests cover the gating, and that a refused or failed attempt records its reason without ever advancing the last-success clock. Three changes on review, all the same principle: the job must not report safety it is not providing. The staleness caveat was on only one branch, so a five-day-old backup rendered as a bare date and read as a daily one. Both branches now say it only checks while the app is open, because MIN_INTERVAL_MS is a floor on attempts, never a promise of freshness. checkNow swallowed throws. runIfDue reaches Play Services and writes prefs, either of which can throw, and inside a launch on a SupervisorJob that vanishes with nothing logged and nothing shown, leaving the screen displaying the last SUCCESS as though no attempt had been made. It now records the throw as a failure reason and surfaces it in words. Its doc claimed it never throws. Corrected rather than left to mislead. Also repointed two androidTest files that cited the just-deleted supersede test as precedent for "a JVM test cannot reach this" - that file had proved the opposite by moving to Robolectric, and leaving the citation would propagate the stale reasoning the port removed. Verified on the current tree: compileDebugKotlin -Pnokey, testDebugUnitTest and compileDebugAndroidTestKotlin all green, 2,549 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped, counted from the JUnit XML. NOT verified: a real Drive upload, a real 24h-later foreground trigger, or the screen's wording on a device. No device is attached to this machine. backend-erp 01backend-erp 03backend-erp 05
43107cf · 7 files
Three rulings and a seven-phase sequence. The map closes with all six tickets resolved and nothing built. SyncEngine retires per-table rather than wholesale: each table leaves the Drive registry in the same commit its writes move to Postgres. The rule that makes it safe is that no table is ever in two sync channels, because Drive's strictly-greater LWW and Postgres would otherwise fight silently over the same rows while both looked healthy. The Item-into-Event merge lands directly in the Supabase schema. That is forced rather than chosen: there is no legacy events table to fall back to, since Dates was born engine-native. Ticket 01's repoint-to-existing-tables shortcut covers ledger, pantry, fleet and places but not Notes and Dates, whose target has to be built new either way. Kevin chose schema-and-auth first over a thin vertical slice. The accepted risk is written down rather than smoothed over: the stack is unproven until the first aspect lands. Running aspects smallest-first mitigates it for free, so Places and its three records is the de-facto proving run. Two clarifications in the ticket exist to prevent specific mistakes. Ticket 03's "engine retirement before or with the RPC" does not mean deleting 15,885 lines up front - the server schema is typed from day one so the RPC is never built against the generic shape, while the phone's engine retires per aspect. And legacy-table drops no longer mean what they did, because ruling 7 sends the phone back to those very tables; they are the destination, not drop candidates. Deletion is deliberately separated from retirement throughout, for one reason: every rollback depends on the code deleted at the end still existing during the middle. Ticket 03 resolved: one idempotent RPC, and the statement parsers retire
backend-erp 01backend-erp 03backend-erp 05
293e4d3 · 10 files
Eight rulings. Two of them change things outside this ticket. The commit becomes a single Supabase RPC, idempotent on the file's content hash. That idempotency is not a nicety: ticket 01's ruling 8 removed the offline queue, so a network death after Postgres commits but before the ack leaves the phone unable to tell success from failure, and AriaBrain's CANNOT_CLAUSE is binary - a tool result is successful or it is nothing, with no vocabulary for "unknown". Making the RPC a successful no-op on repeat means the phone retries until the answer is definitive instead of narrating a state it cannot describe honestly. Gate arithmetic runs server-side with the phone pre-checking, which buys a fast local fail at the cost of two implementations that must not drift. The larger change is Kevin's own proposal: the deterministic statement parsers retire. A statement goes through the user's own LLM, which masks sensitive data and emits a CSV in a format LEGION defines. That kills PdfBox and with it the Deno problem, covers every bank rather than only DBS and BofA, and puts masking before upload, which matters more now the truth lives in a cloud Postgres. It amends CLAUDE.md section 4 rule 1, and the amendment is written in there, marked decided-but-not-built so nobody reads the parsers as already gone. The gate gets stronger to pay for it. An LLM-produced CSV has its lines and its total from one nondeterministic process, so a single anchor could be satisfied by a hallucination that hallucinated its own total to match - rule 6's failure shape in a new place. The format therefore demands three separately printed anchors, and a statement carrying fewer falls to rule 7 provisional instead. Ticket 01's ruling 10 is amended the same day: photo files may leave the device, to a private bucket in the household's own project, because Edge-Function receipt vision cannot work otherwise. The other three stay phone-only. Three pre-existing defects are filed on the ticket rather than lost, the sharpest being that the four tests covering rule-7 supersession have not touched production code since cutover 3. backend-erp 02backend-erp 05

Five rulings, and one correction to the ticket's own premise. The premise first: the ticket said the app "already has Google sign-in plumbing for Drive." It does not. DriveAuth uses the Google Identity Authorization API for one drive.appdata scope and stores no token, no account, no email - sign-out is a boolean flip. There is no human-user entity anywhere in the app and no table has a human owner column. Google sign-in would have been built from scratch. That removed the main argument for it, and the remaining two options each carry a documented trap: Google OAuth needs two client IDs with one keyed to the SHA-1 signing cert, the same trap already open against Drive; magic link rides Supabase's built-in email at 2 messages per hour, which its own docs call not meant for production with no delivery SLA. Email+password touches neither. That limit is now recorded as section 7b of the feasibility research, traced to the primary source. The rest: household visibility with RLS through a household_members table, no roles ever. Both accounts made in the dashboard - no signup screen, no invite flow, zero app code. Personas and memories bind to the user rather than the device, and memories gain a user tag, because recalling one person's statement as the other's is precisely the unfalsifiable-memory failure CLAUDE.md section 7 forbids. The session goes in KeyVault but fails closed - no plaintext fallback, unlike every other secret slot. That fallback exists for cheap head units with flaky keymaster, and phone-only killed the reason. A refresh token is not a Gemini key; it is a standing credential to all household data. Resume at ticket 03. Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

MUST-FIX: reconcileSupersededProvisional trashed any active engine UNRECONCILED row whose guid was missing from legacy allSyncIds(). Post- cutover, IngestPipeline.commit/LedgerController.logPendingTransaction create brand-new engine UNRECONCILED rows whose guid never touched the legacy table - always missing by construction. A driver importing a CSV or voice-logging a pending transaction on first launch, before the fire-and-forget catchUpOnce coroutine finishes, would have that legitimate row silently trashed. Fixed with a persisted migrated-guid set (migrated_guids_v1): copyLedgerIfNeeded records every guid it confirms as legacy-derived, and reconcileSupersededProvisional gates on membership in that set before ever checking legacy presence. A createdAt-cutoff was considered and rejected: both the copier and IngestPipeline's own create call pass now = txn.txnDate to RecordStore.create, so createdAt reflects the transaction's own date for both migrated and live rows, never wall-clock insert time - a timestamp comparison would have been silently wrong on real data. New tests: catchUpOnce never trashes an engine-native row whose guid was never in the legacy table, even if created before reconcile runs (the race itself); catchUpOnce still trashes a genuinely migrated row once its legacy backing disappears, proving the new gate isn't overbroad (positive control). SHOULD-FIX: RecordStore._afterWrite.tryEmit fires inside the caller's withTransaction. Traced rather than changed - the only production subscriber always routes through MirrorSync.scheduleExport(), which delays 5 seconds and reads fresh via DAO calls at read time, well past any ledger/pantry multi-row transaction's settle time, and independent of that margin Room's own transactional isolation means a reader outside a transaction cannot observe its uncommitted writes. Documented in RecordStore.kt's afterWrite doc comment. No test: a genuine cross-connection commit/rollback race is not something Robolectric's single-process SQLite harness can be trusted to reproduce meaningfully. Suite green both key ways. voice_guide.py exit 0.
